1. Understanding the Architecture

For a SuccessFactors implementation, the Joule landscape can be viewed in three layers.

Experience Layer

The user works primarily in SAP SuccessFactors.

Joule is embedded into the SuccessFactors user experience. Users don't need to leave SuccessFactors simply to interact with Joule. [https://le...essfactors]

Conceptually:

Employee / Manager → SAP SuccessFactors → SAP Joule

AI and Platform Layer

Although Joule appears inside SuccessFactors, Joule itself runs as a service on SAP BTP. [https://le...essfactors]

SAP SuccessFactors continues to own the HR business data and processes, while Joule provides the conversational and orchestration layer.

Conceptually:

SAP SuccessFactors → SAP Joule → SAP BTP

Identity and Authorization Layer

The third area is identity and authorization.

SAP Cloud Identity Services forms part of the Joule identity architecture, while SAP SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions determine which SuccessFactors information and functionality a user is authorized to access. [https://le...essfactors]

This separation is important. Enabling Joule does not give the user unrestricted access to SuccessFactors.

2. Check the Prerequisites

Before configuring anything, start by validating that your landscape satisfies SAP's Joule prerequisites.

SAP's Setting Up Joule for SAP SuccessFactors Learning content lists prerequisites including:

  • SAP BTP account with the required Joule entitlement
  • Joule entitlement identified as das-application
  • SAP SuccessFactors license
  • Joule availability for the applicable data center
  • SAP Cloud Identity Services with active tenants
  • SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition / SAP Start [https://le...essfactors]

The last prerequisite is worth noting.

Your users may access Joule directly from the SuccessFactors experience and may not use a separate SAP Build Work Zone site as their business launchpad. Nevertheless, SAP's current Learning material lists SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition / SAP Start among the prerequisites for the overall Joule setup. [https://le...essfactors]

Therefore, don't interpret "using SuccessFactors as the launchpad" as meaning that all SAP Start / Build Work Zone platform dependencies can simply be omitted.

Follow the dependencies presented by the Joule onboarding process for your particular landscape.

3. Check the Required Administrator Access

Before starting the implementation, make sure the configuration team has the required administrative access.

SAP's SuccessFactors Joule setup guidance identifies the following administrative roles:

  • SAP SuccessFactors Administrator
  • SAP BTP Global Account Administrator
  • SAP Cloud Identity Services Administrator [https://he...cale=en-US]

This is important because the onboarding isn't limited to SuccessFactors configuration. It crosses the SuccessFactors, BTP and identity landscapes.

At this stage, your initial checklist should therefore be:

  • SuccessFactors tenant and license are available
  • SAP BTP Global Account is identified
  • Joule entitlement is available
  • Appropriate SAP Cloud Identity Services tenants are available
  • Required administrators have access
  • Joule availability for the relevant landscape/data center has been checked
  • SAP Start / Build Work Zone requirement has been assessed according to the current Joule onboarding model

4. Verify the Joule Entitlement in SAP BTP

The next step is to verify that the SAP BTP Global Account has the required Joule entitlement.

SAP Learning specifically identifies the Joule entitlement as:

das-application

SAP recommends checking the entitlements available in the BTP Global Account. [https://le...essfactors]

If you have the appropriate SuccessFactors license but the Joule entitlement isn't available, SAP Learning advises contacting your SAP Account Executive. [https://le...essfactors]

Don't try to compensate for a missing Joule entitlement by manually creating unrelated BTP services. Resolve the commercial/provisioning issue first.

A successful implementation starts with the correct entitlement being delivered to the correct SAP BTP Global Account.

5. Prepare SAP Cloud Identity Services

Once the commercial and BTP prerequisites are established, the next major area is identity.

SAP Learning explicitly lists SAP Cloud Identity Services with active tenants as a prerequisite for the SuccessFactors Joule scenario. [https://le...essfactors]

Before starting Joule onboarding, document the participating systems and identity landscape.

At minimum, identify:

  • SAP SuccessFactors tenant
  • SAP Cloud Identity Services tenant
  • SAP BTP Global Account
  • Relevant BTP landscape
  • Production versus non-production systems
  • User identities used across the participating systems

This might seem administrative, but it becomes extremely useful when troubleshooting authentication and user provisioning.

A common source of confusion is treating IAS and IPS as though they perform the same function. They should be considered separately.

6. Understand IAS: Identity Authentication

SAP Identity Authentication is part of SAP Cloud Identity Services.

From an implementation perspective, think about Identity Authentication as the authentication side of the architecture.

The central question is:

How is the identity of the user established across the participating SAP applications?

Your Joule implementation therefore needs to consider how SuccessFactors, Joule/BTP and SAP Cloud Identity Services participate in establishing a consistent user identity.

SAP's Learning material identifies active SAP Cloud Identity Services tenants as part of the prerequisites for the SuccessFactors Joule scenario. [https://le...essfactors]

The exact configuration should follow the Joule onboarding guidance appropriate to your tenant rather than assuming a generic IAS configuration will be sufficient.

7. Understand IPS: Identity Provisioning

Authentication isn't the whole identity story.

The second area is Identity Provisioning Service (IPS).

Conceptually:

IAS answers the authentication/identity question.

IPS deals with provisioning identities between the relevant systems.

SAP's Joule provisioning documentation explicitly includes Configure Identity Provisioning Service within the SuccessFactors integration area. [https://he...cale=en-US]

Therefore, don't document your implementation simply as "IAS configured."

Your architecture documentation should separately record:

Authentication

How users authenticate and how their identities are established across the participating applications.

Provisioning

How identities required by the Joule landscape are provisioned and synchronized.

The actual source, target and provisioning configuration should follow the current SAP Joule Onboarding Guide for the landscape being implemented.

8. Start the Official Joule Onboarding Process

Once the prerequisites, BTP entitlement and Cloud Identity Services landscape are ready, proceed with Joule onboarding.

This is an area where it is especially important not to follow an outdated blog containing a static list of destinations, service instances or role collections.

SAP's current SuccessFactors documentation directs administrators to:

Follow the Joule Onboarding Guide to finish the setup. [https://he...cale=en-US]

SAP Learning also points to SAP's activation guidance for implementing Joule with SuccessFactors. [https://le...essfactors]

Use the official onboarding process applicable to your system.

During this phase, validate that you are working with:

  • The intended BTP Global Account
  • The intended SuccessFactors system
  • The correct SAP Cloud Identity Services landscape
  • The required Joule entitlement
  • The appropriate production or non-production environment

Avoid manually reproducing configuration from an old implementation unless that configuration is still explicitly required by the current onboarding process.

9. Understand the Role of SAP Build Work Zone / SAP Start

This particular topic can create confusion for SuccessFactors customers.

In this implementation scenario, the end user experiences Joule through SAP SuccessFactors.

That does not mean you should automatically remove SAP Build Work Zone/SAP Start from the technical architecture.

SAP's current Learning material for setting up Joule with SuccessFactors explicitly lists:

SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition / SAP Start

among the prerequisites. [https://le...essfactors]

The accurate way to describe the architecture is therefore:

SuccessFactors is the user-facing business application from which users interact with Joule. The technical services and platform dependencies required by SAP's current Joule onboarding model are provisioned separately according to SAP's onboarding guidance.

This is particularly important if you're coming from an S/4HANA Cloud background.

Don't equate the user's launchpad with every underlying platform component used to deliver Joule.

10. Complete the SuccessFactors-Side Joule Setup

After completing the required Joule onboarding activities, move to the SuccessFactors-side configuration.

The critical concept here is that provisioning Joule doesn't automatically give every SuccessFactors user access to it.

You still need to control which users have permission to use Joule.

SAP's SuccessFactors documentation explicitly identifies an Access to Joule permission. [https://he...cale=en-US]

In SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions, the documented permission is located under:

User Permissions → General User Permission → Access to Joule [https://he...cale=en-US]

Assign this permission through the appropriate SuccessFactors RBP roles according to the users who should have access to Joule.

This gives you a clear separation:

Technical onboarding enables the Joule service.

SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions control which SuccessFactors users can access Joule.

11. Existing SuccessFactors Authorizations Still Apply

Granting Access to Joule should not be confused with granting unrestricted access to SuccessFactors functionality.

SAP states that the business data and actions accessed through Joule continue to be governed by existing SuccessFactors authorizations. [https://le...essfactors]

This means two conditions need to be considered.

Condition 1: Joule access

Is the user authorized to access Joule?

Condition 2: Business authorization

Is the same user authorized in SuccessFactors to access the requested HR information or execute the requested business operation?

Both are important.

For example, enabling Joule for an employee should not be considered a mechanism for bypassing Role-Based Permissions protecting manager or HR information.

This is one of the most important design principles to explain to your security and HR authorization teams.

12. Configure Employee Central Quick Actions Where Applicable

If you're using SAP SuccessFactors Employee Central, there is another configuration area to review.

SAP recommends enabling Employee Central Quick Actions and configuring the corresponding templates for Employee Central customers using Joule. [https://he...cale=en-US]

The reason this is relevant is that Joule isn't purely a question-and-answer interface.

SAP's architecture description discusses Joule supporting conversational interaction involving navigation and transactional interactions in the business application. [https://le...essfactors]

Therefore, for Employee Central implementations, review the Quick Actions needed for the supported Joule use cases you intend to make available.

Don't assume that every Employee Central action automatically becomes available through Joule.

Always validate the particular use case against the current SuccessFactors Joule documentation.

13. Validate Joule in SAP SuccessFactors

Once the onboarding, identity configuration and SuccessFactors authorization settings are complete, validate the solution from the SuccessFactors experience.

Use a test user that has:

  • Access to Joule
  • Correct identity configuration
  • Appropriate SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions
  • Access to the underlying SuccessFactors functionality being tested

The first validation is simple:

Can the user access Joule from the SuccessFactors user experience?

If yes, don't stop there.

The next validation is:

Can Joule access only the SuccessFactors information and operations that this user is authorized to use?

SAP states that existing SuccessFactors authorizations govern the data and actions available through Joule. [https://le...essfactors]

That means functional and security validation should be performed together.

14. Test Different Authorization Scenarios

A good implementation should test more than one type of user.

Employee User

Use an employee account with normal Employee Self-Service permissions.

Validate the supported Joule scenarios applicable to employees.

Manager User

Use a manager account with appropriate manager permissions.

Validate supported manager scenarios where applicable.

Restricted User

Use an account intentionally lacking access to selected SuccessFactors information or functionality.

Validate that giving the user access to Joule doesn't extend the user's access beyond the underlying SuccessFactors authorization.

The purpose is not merely to prove that Joule opens successfully.

The purpose is to prove:

Joule availability + correct identity + correct SuccessFactors authorization + supported use case

work together.

15. Understand Which SuccessFactors Use Cases Are Supported

Another important implementation step is determining what you actually want users to do with Joule.

Not every SuccessFactors capability should be assumed to have a corresponding Joule capability.

SAP maintains documentation for the supported Joule capabilities and use cases within SuccessFactors. [https://he...essfactors]

For example, SAP's SuccessFactors Onboarding documentation lists scenarios such as:

  • Completing required onboarding tasks
  • Assigning a buddy
  • Viewing pending offboarding tasks
  • Directing new hires to their Onboarding Checklist and Onboarding Guide [https://he...cale=en-US]

This demonstrates why the business configuration underneath Joule remains important.

Having the Joule window available doesn't automatically make every HR operation available conversationally.

For any implementation, create a list of the specific SuccessFactors Joule use cases that your organization plans to enable and validate each against current SAP documentation.

16. End-to-End Implementation Sequence

Putting everything together, the recommended implementation flow is:

Step 1: Verify SuccessFactors prerequisites

Confirm the SuccessFactors licensing and applicable Joule prerequisites.

Step 2: Verify Joule availability

Check whether Joule is available for the applicable SuccessFactors landscape/data center according to the current SAP guidance. [https://le...essfactors]

Step 3: Verify the BTP Global Account

Confirm that you're working with the intended SAP BTP Global Account.

Step 4: Verify Joule entitlement

Check that the Joule das-application entitlement is available in the BTP landscape. [https://le...essfactors]

If the entitlement is missing for an appropriately licensed scenario, follow SAP's guidance and contact the SAP Account Executive. [https://le...essfactors]

Step 5: Establish the SAP Cloud Identity Services landscape

Identify the SAP Cloud Identity Services tenant participating in the implementation. SAP lists active Cloud Identity Services tenants among the SuccessFactors Joule prerequisites. [https://le...essfactors]

Step 6: Address authentication

Follow the Joule onboarding guidance for the required Identity Authentication configuration.

Step 7: Address identity provisioning

Configure the required Identity Provisioning integration according to the current onboarding flow. SAP's Joule provisioning documentation includes Identity Provisioning configuration within the SuccessFactors integration area. [https://he...cale=en-US]

Step 8: Complete Joule onboarding

Follow the official Joule Onboarding Guide, as directed by SAP's SuccessFactors documentation. [https://he...cale=en-US]

Step 9: Handle SAP Start / Build Work Zone dependencies

Implement the applicable platform dependency according to the Joule onboarding model. SAP's current Learning content lists SAP Build Work Zone, standard edition / SAP Start as a prerequisite. [https://le...essfactors]

This doesn't mean users must use a separate Work Zone site as their SuccessFactors launchpad.

Step 10: Configure SuccessFactors Joule access

Grant the relevant SuccessFactors users:

User Permissions → General User Permission → Access to Joule [https://he...cale=en-US]

Step 11: Review SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions

Ensure users have the underlying SuccessFactors authorization required by each business use case. Joule continues to operate within these authorization boundaries. [https://le...essfactors]

Step 12: Configure Employee Central Quick Actions where applicable

For Employee Central scenarios, review and configure the Quick Actions recommended by SAP. [https://he...cale=en-US]

Step 13: Validate Joule

Test Joule from the SAP SuccessFactors user experience.

Step 14: Validate business use cases

Test the actual supported employee and manager use cases required by your organization.

Step 15: Validate authorization boundaries

Confirm that Joule respects the underlying SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions.

17. Troubleshooting Approach

If Joule isn't working after configuration, troubleshoot the solution layer by layer instead of changing multiple components simultaneously.

Joule isn't available at all

First verify:

  • Joule entitlement
  • BTP landscape
  • Joule onboarding completion
  • SuccessFactors Access to Joule permission

User can't access Joule

Verify:

  • User identity
  • Relevant Cloud Identity Services configuration
  • Identity provisioning
  • SuccessFactors Access to Joule permission

Joule opens but a business request doesn't work

Verify:

  • Whether that particular Joule use case is supported
  • User's SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions
  • Required SuccessFactors business configuration
  • Employee Central Quick Actions where applicable

This layer-by-layer troubleshooting method is my recommended implementation approach. The individual requirements above should still be validated against the current SAP onboarding documentation.

18. Final Implementation Checklist

Before declaring the solution ready, validate the following.

Licensing and Landscape

  • SuccessFactors license verified
  • Joule availability verified
  • Correct BTP Global Account identified
  • Correct landscape selected
  • Joule das-application entitlement available

Identity

  • SAP Cloud Identity Services available
  • Authentication requirements completed according to Joule onboarding
  • Identity provisioning requirements completed
  • User identity is consistent across the participating landscape

Joule

  • Official Joule onboarding completed
  • Required platform services provisioned
  • SuccessFactors integration completed

SuccessFactors

  • Access to Joule permission assigned
  • Target users correctly included in RBP roles
  • Underlying SuccessFactors permissions validated
  • Employee Central Quick Actions configured where applicable

Validation

  • Joule accessible from SuccessFactors
  • Employee scenario validated
  • Manager scenario validated where applicable
  • Restricted-user scenario validated
  • RBP authorization boundaries confirmed
  • Required SuccessFactors Joule use cases tested

Conclusion

The most important point when implementing Joule for SAP SuccessFactors is understanding that this isn't simply a switch inside SuccessFactors.

The implementation spans multiple layers:

SAP SuccessFactors provides the HR business application and remains the system of record.

SAP Joule on SAP BTP provides the conversational AI and orchestration experience.

SAP Cloud Identity Services participates in the identity architecture.

SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions continue to control access to HR data and business functionality. [https://le...essfactors]

For users, however, the experience can remain straightforward: they interact with Joule from SAP SuccessFactors while the underlying BTP and identity landscape provides the services required to enable that experience.

For implementation teams, the safest sequence is therefore:

Prerequisites → Entitlement → Identity → Provisioning → Joule Onboarding → SuccessFactors Permissions → Quick Actions → Business Use Cases → Security Validation

Most importantly, always use the current SAP Joule Onboarding Guide for the tenant being implemented instead of relying exclusively on older manual configuration procedures. SAP's current SuccessFactors documentation explicitly directs administrators to the Joule Onboarding Guide for setup. [https://he...cale=en-US]

entry.title: What If Joule Could Help You Complete the Business-Driven Configuration Questionnaire? Now It Can.
entry.content:
A successful SAP S/4HANA Cloud implementation starts with understanding how a business works—and translating that understanding into the right configuration. The Business-Driven Configuration Questionnaire (BDCQ), a structured accelerator within the SAP Activate methodology, helps make that connection. Line of Business (LoB) configuration experts use it to gather the configuration values that will ultimately be entered in SAP Central Business Configuration for the customer’s SAP S/4HANA Cloud development system tenants.

More than a questionnaire, the BDCQ is a bridge between SAP consultants and customer business users. It helps ensure that solution configuration reflects real business requirements, both before and during Fit-to-Standard workshops.

Why does the BDCQ matter?

  • It provides early insight into the customer’s business processes and configuration needs.
  • It offers prescriptive guidance on identifying configuration requirements aligned with the implementation scope.
  • It provides a secondary validation of whether SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition (Public Cloud) is the right fit for the customer, complementing the Digital Discovery Assessment (DDA).
  • It brings greater structure to the planning and delivery of Fit-to-Standard Analysis workshops.
  • It supports productive conversations between implementation experts and business users during workshops.
  • It connects customer business processes directly to solution configuration activities, including references to specific SSCUI apps or SSCUI groups.

The BDCQ captures two levels of information at different stages of the project:

The value of the BDCQ goes beyond collecting configuration data. It also helps LoB configuration experts build relationships with customer LoB experts and introduces those experts to SAP S/4HANA Cloud early in the project. Ideally, the same customer experts who provide L2 responses will take part in Fit-to-Standard workshops and user acceptance testing before go-live. In this way, the BDCQ also supports the project’s broader change-management effort.

Not every BDCQ maps neatly to a traditional line of business. The implementation team should therefore confirm that all business processes selected in the Digital Discovery Assessment are covered across the available BDCQs. Any remaining processes—for example, Human Resources or Two-Tier ERP—should be assigned based on transferable expertise and team availability.

So, how can AI-assisted support make it easier to complete the BDCQ?

During the Prepare phase, open Perform Initial Business Process Assessment for SAP S/4HANA Cloud. You’ll find the ✦ AI-Assisted Procedure session there.

Open the session and follow the instructions for working with the BDCQ Experts.

For example, the BDCQ-FI Expert can guide you through the questionnaire in a conversational manner. Start the conversation, answer its questions, and review the highlights and key points that deserve attention. This provides structured support as you work through the information required for your BDCQ.

The result is a BDCQ populated with Critical Steps, Scope Items, open items, and potential blockers—as illustrated in the example below.

entry.title: Did You Know? An SAP Business Data Cloud Series | Season 1, Episode 3 | Joule for Datasphere
entry.content:
Your AI Copilot Is Already Inside SAP Datasphere... Are You Using It? 

Here's something a lot of SAP Datasphere users don't realize: Joule, SAP's generative AI copilot, is embedded directly in Datasphere. Not in a separate tool, but directly in the platform you're already working on every day. 

Many data professionals associate Joule with SAP S/4HANA or SAP Analytics Cloud. And while Joule is also present in those products, its integration with Datasphere is one of the more quietly powerful capabilities in your SAP Business Data Cloud environment. 

What is Joule for Datasphere? 

Joule in Datasphere supports three categories of tasks: informational, navigational, and transactional. Together, they cover a meaningful slice of the day-to-day work data professionals do inside the tool. 

Informational: Ask Joule how to use a specific Datasphere feature and get an answer grounded in product documentation without leaving the platform to hunt through help pages or community posts. You can also query Joule for instance-specific information about your own Datasphere environment. 

Navigational: Joule can guide you through tasks and help you move around the platform more efficiently. For newer team members or occasional users, this can significantly reduce the learning curve. 

Transactional: This is where it gets genuinely interesting for data engineers and modelers. Joule supports AI-assisted SQL generation directly in the SQL View Builder. This means that you can describe what you want in natural language, and Joule generates the SQL. Whether you're creating a new SQL view from scratch or modifying an existing one, this capability can meaningfully cut down the time spent writing and debugging queries. 

Joule also supports AI-assisted semantic generation, automatically recognizing and assigning semantic types for ingested non-SAP data, which is typically a manual and time-consuming preparation step. 

Why it Matters to Data Professionals 

The honest reality of working with data at scale is that a significant portion of the time goes into maintenance tasks: figuring out the right syntax, navigating documentation, writing boilerplate SQL, manually classifying fields. These tasks take valuable time out of your day and eat into time that could be spent making strategic business decisions. Joule helps give you that time back! It doesn't replace your judgment, but rather it takes on the mechanical parts, so you can focus on the work that actually requires your expertise. 

For data modelers, the SQL generation capability alone is worth exploring. For enterprise architects managing complex environments with many users at different skill levels, the informational and navigational capabilities help teams work more independently and consistently. 

Why You May Have Missed It 

Joule in Datasphere needs to be activated at the tenant level and requires users to have the appropriate privilege assigned. It doesn't switch on automatically. That setup step means a lot of teams have Joule available but haven't enabled it, or have enabled it without communicating it to the people who would benefit most. 

If you're a Datasphere administrator reading this, it's worth checking whether Joule is active in your environment and whether your modelers and data engineers know it's there. 

See It in Action

Give it a try in your own environment and see how much of your workflow it can simplify.  

Already using Joule in Datasphere? Drop a comment below! I'd love to hear how your team is putting it to work.

entry.title: SAP CPQ : The Future of Sales Quoting Is Here: Meet SAP's Joule Quoting Assistant & Other Agents
entry.content:
Disclaimer: : The purpose of this blog is to share a custom implementation approach for automating sales processes in SAP CPQ using Joule Work and Joule Studio. This content is aimed at customers and partners interested in innovation and automation scenarios.  
If you would like to explore these capabilities, please enroll in the EAC program and connect with your SAP CSM, CSP, or Account Executive to discuss available options.

Also please watch out for the Official SAP CPQ Product Roadmap items for Joule Assistants Delivery and What's New for SAP CPQ releases time to time.

How AI is transforming one of sales' most time-consuming processes

Every sales rep knows the pain. A customer sends over an email — or a ten-page PDF — and suddenly you're spending the better part of your afternoon manually parsing the request, matching products, checking pricing rules, and assembling a proposal document. It's repetitive, error-prone, and it gets in the way of actual selling.

SAP's Joule Quoting Assistant & remaining 6 other Agents is designed to change that entirely.

What Is the Joule Quoting Assistant?

The Joule Quoting Assistant is an AI-powered Joule Assistant — part of SAP's broader agentic AI portfolio — built specifically for the quote-to-order cycle. Its core mission: transform unstructured customer requests into accurate, compliant quotes with AI-guided selling across the entire SAP CPQ (Configure, Price, Quote) flow. Source

It sits at the intersection of SAP CPQ, SAP Sales Cloud, and SAP S/4HANA, orchestrating specialized AI agents behind the scenes to handle tasks that would otherwise fall to the sales rep or a back-office support team.

From Inbox to Quote: What It Actually Does

Here's where the Quoting Assistant gets practical. Given an unstructured customer inquiry — whether it arrives as an email, a request for quotation (RFQ), or a PDF — the assistant can:

  • Convert the raw request into a structured CPQ quote draft, extracting relevant intent and mapping it to your product catalog and pricing rules.
  • Recommend compliant product configurations based on what the customer described in natural language — no need to manually navigate complex configurators.
  • Surface real-time upsell, add-on, and cross-sell options guided by historical deal data and pricing policies.
  • Assemble proposal documents and draft customer-facing emails, ready for the rep to review and send.
  • Route multi-step requests to the right specialized agents automatically, without manual handoffs.
  • Enforce pricing and discount policies — every quote stays within guardrails, reducing approvals overhead and compliance risk. Source

Why This Matters for your Sales Teams

The shift from manual quoting to AI-guided quoting isn't just about speed — it changes the quality and consistency of the entire sales conversation.

Faster time to first draft. Instead of spending hours building a quote from scratch, reps get an intelligent draft that's already shaped by the customer's actual request. That frees them up to focus on relationship management and deal strategy.

Better accuracy and compliance. When pricing rules, discount limits, and configuration constraints are embedded in the assistant's reasoning, errors are caught before they reach the customer — not after an internal audit.

Higher deal size through guided selling. Real-time upsell and cross-sell recommendations aren't an afterthought; they're built into the quoting flow. Reps are prompted with relevant options at exactly the right moment.

Tighter SAP ecosystem integration. The Quoting Assistant works natively within SAP CPQ and SAP S/4HANA, which means no data re-entry, clean-core alignment, and full traceability across the quote lifecycle. Source

The Architecture Behind It: Assistants + Agents

The Quoting Assistant doesn't work alone. It's part of SAP's layered AI architecture: Joule Assistants — role-aligned, context-aware AI systems — sit above Joule Agents, which are the task specialists that execute individual steps. Source

You tell the Quoting Assistant what you want to accomplish in plain language. It interprets your intent, pulls in your business context (your CPQ rules, your pricing policies, your customer history), and coordinates the agents doing the actual work. You stay in control; the heavy lifting happens automatically.

This architecture is important because it means the Quoting Assistant isn't a standalone tool — it's part of SAP's Autonomous Enterprise vision, where AI handles routine execution so people can focus on decisions that require judgment.

A Real-World Scenario

Imagine a key account manager receives an email from a customer requesting a customised bundle of hardware and professional services across three countries, with specific delivery windows and a tight margin requirement.

Historically, this would take hours — coordinating with product management, pricing, and legal before a quote could even be drafted.

With the Joule Quoting Assistant, the rep pastes (or forwards) the customer email, and the assistant:

  1. Parses the request and maps it to available products and service SKUs.
  2. Checks configuration rules and flags any incompatible options.
  3. Proposes a compliant price structure with margin guardrails.
  4. Recommends a maintenance bundle and a support tier upsell.
  5. Drafts the proposal document and a personalised cover email.

The rep reviews, adjusts, approves. What took half a day now takes minutes.

What This Signals for the Future of Sales

SAP's investment in the Quoting Assistant reflects a broader industry shift: the sales rep of the near future is a reviewer and relationship manager, not a data entry clerk. AI handles the structure; humans handle the nuance.

For organisations running SAP CPQ or SAP Sales Cloud v2, this isn't a distant roadmap item — it's available now, and it integrates with the systems you already have. The question isn't whether to evaluate it; it's how quickly you can get it into the hands of your team.

The SAP Joule Quoting Assistant is part of the SAP Joule Assistants portfolio. Learn more at sap.com/use-cases/joule-assistant/quoting-ai.

entry.content:
SAP Business AI can look like a shopping list: Joule, Joule Work, Joule Studio, Business Data Cloud, Knowledge Graph, AI Agent Hub. This post explains what each piece does and how they fit together.

The Big Picture

SAP’s Business AI Platform is built on three pillars: Build, Contextualize and Reason, and Govern.

 

The Components in Plain Language

 

How They Work Together

A user states a goal in Joule Work. An Assistant picks the right Agents. The agents use the Knowledge Graph and Business Data Cloud for context and run inside the Autonomous Suite. The Agent Gateway enforces permissions at each step, and the AI Agent Hub keeps every agent visible and governed.

Why This Is Not a Chatbot

 

 

 

A Short Example (illustrative)

User types in Joule Work: “A key customer reported a damaged delivery. Check replacement stock and update the service case.”

 

 

The user never opens five applications. This scenario is my own illustration, not an SAP-documented use case. Both assistants are named in SAP’s Sapphire 2026 guide, but check their current availability before promising them to a customer.

Open by Design

Agents built in Joule Studio natively support the MCP and A2A protocols to work with third-party tools and agents. Customers are not locked into agents built only by SAP.

Why This Matter

  • Data and process readiness → grounding through Knowledge Graph and Business Data Cloud
  • Custom capability → Joule Studio (low-code) or pro-code agents on SAP BTP
  • Governance and risk → identity, Agent Gateway and AI Agent Hub
  • Adoption → moving users from “navigate screens” to “state goals”

AI quality is limited by data quality. A strong platform on weak master data gives weak results.

Key Takeaways

  • The platform rests on three pillars: Build, Contextualize and Reason, Govern.
  • Joule Work is what users see. Grounding and governance make it trustworthy.
  • Assistants coordinate, agents execute, and the gateway enforces permissions.
  • MCP and A2A keep the architecture open.
  • Clean data and clear process ownership matter as much as the technology.

Closing Thought

Before asking “Which Joule feature should we activate?”, ask: “Is our data, process ownership and governance ready for AI to act on our behalf?”

entry.title: From static plans to a “planning brain”: how SAP planning agents can reshape Enterprise Planning
entry.content:
Introduction

The opportunity with planning agents is not simply to produce forecasts faster. It is to connect the work of preparing data, building models, investigating performance, evaluating scenarios and communicating decisions.

SAP Analytics Cloud Planning provides the planning engine at the centre of this approach. SAP Enterprise Planning extends that foundation with SAP-managed domain content, curated data products, SAP Datasphere, and performance steering capabilities powered by SAP Business Data Cloud. Together, they support a direction towards more continuous, AI-assisted planning and decision-making.

The perspective below brings together AI assistants, agents and powerful performance-sensing-and-steering capabilities. The accompanying illustration indicates a phased roadmap and the innovation at SAP continues.

For planners, the intended shift is from spending most of their time assembling the answer to spending more time challenging assumptions, evaluating trade-offs and steering business performance.

1. Why planning needs to move beyond the calendar

Budgets, quarterly forecasts and monthly performance reviews give organisations structure. But the conditions behind those plans do not wait for the next planning cycle.

Demand changes. Input costs move. Hiring assumptions shift. A customer delays an order. Each event can affect revenue, margin, capacity and cash—but the implications may sit across different teams and planning models.

The challenge is not just to detect a change. It is to connect that change to a decision:

  • What has moved?

  • Why does it matter?

  • Which assumptions need revisiting?

  • What options do we have?

  • Who needs to approve the response?

SAP’s direction addresses this gap through agents that monitor internal and external signals, assess deviations against KPIs and planning assumptions, and help evaluate appropriate responses. Periodic planning remains important; continuous steering adds a way to respond between those cycles.

2. The big picture: a connected planning brain

SAP Analytics Cloud Planning is at the centre of three connected elements:

  1. The planning foundation: models, versions, assumptions, calculations and planning processes.

  2. SAP Planning and Analytics agents: specialised assistance across preparation, modelling, analysis, simulation and communication.

  3. Performance Steeing intelligence: identifying changing conditions and coordinating the planning response.

Joule Work is shown as part of the experience connecting users with this planning environment. The eight-step process beneath the architecture connects the technology to the business lifecycle - from setting targets through forecasting, alignment, performance analysis and executive storytelling.

The “planning brain” is a useful way to describe the relationship between these elements. I am representing this as a planning environment in which data, business logic, analysis and actions become more closely connected. SAP Analytics Cloud Planning is the core planning engine delivering Enterprise-wise Financial and Extended Planning capabilities.

3. Planning and Analytics agents across the planning lifecycle

The agents in the illustration above address different aspects of planning work. The table below summarises their intended contribution at a business level; exact capabilities and availability should be checked against the current roadmap and released documentation as these reach SAP General Availability (GA):

 


Agentic CapabilityIntended contribution to planning processesIndicative  timeline*
Enterprise Planning & Simulation AgentAssist with planning activities and scenario exploration.Q4 2026
Data Action Design AgentAssist with designing the calculation logic used in planning processes.Q4 2026
Analytics & Planning Model Creation AgentAssist with translating analytical and planning requirements into model structures.Q4 2026
Data & Analytics Insights AgentSupport the creation of data-driven analytical experiences and insights.Q4 2026
Analytics Narrative AgentHelp turn analytical findings into understandable business narratives.Q4 2026
Plan Data Upload AgentAssist with bringing planning inputs into the planning environment.Q1 2027
*These are roadmap indications, not confirmation of general availability.
 

The distinction between the agents matters. Creating a model is different from designing its calculations. Producing an analytical insight is different from explaining its implications to the CFO's organisation. Preparing a scenario is different from deciding whether the business should adopt it.

The value comes from connecting these activities while keeping their purposes and the associated review responsibilities clear.

The upper layer in my illustration extends the perspective beyond individual planning tasks with a focus on steering with a wider enterprise performance management lens. Further details on this can be found here.

4. What this means across the enterprise planning process

In my illustration, I show eight stages of planning as a typical examaple. Rather than assigning one agent rigidly to each stage, it is more useful to consider the business outcome each stage needs to support.

 
Planning stages where agent-supported work could help bring transformation capabilities to the planner:
Strategise and set targetsBring relevant trends, assumptions and performance context into target discussions.
Predict baselines, collaborate and adjustEstablish starting forecasts and help contributors explore changes to assumptions.
Data validation and controlsHelp prepare inputs and identify issues for review, without replacing validation rules or accountability.
Predictive and scenario modellingExplore alternatives and compare their financial and operational implications.
Budget and plan approval, continuous forecastingPrepare proposed updates and supporting analysis for authorised review.
Consolidate and alignSupport alignment across planning contributions, assumptions and calculations.
Performance analytics and reportingInvestigate deviations and focus attention on material changes.
Executive storytellingTranslate findings into audience-appropriate explanations and decision points.

The above is my illustrative of potential business mapping, not an official assignment of agent capabilities.

Here, “consolidate and align” means bringing planning contributions together in a planning process. Important to note that when this focus on Financial Consolidation in a Statutory, Managerial and Planning context, we have some great updates coming as part of the SAP Enterprise Performance Management Strategy coming up in 2027. 

5. From FP&A to Enterprise Wide Planning: the same decision, viewed across functions

Consider a life sciences enterprise facing softer demand and higher material costs.

From an FP&A perspective, the immediate questions concern revenue, margin, expenditure and cash. But when looking further as an extended enterprise planning perspective, answering those questions requires connected assumptions from sales, procurement, production and workforce planning.

In this new agentic world, an agent-supported workflow could shorten the path from detecting a change to evaluating and approving a response:

>Detect and investigate

A material deviation prompts investigation. Finance and business owners assess whether the change reflects volume, price, mix, timing or cost pressure.

Market context can inform the analysis, but it should not be mistaken for proof of the underlying cause.

>Evaluate alternatives

The team compares responses: adjust production, revise purchasing assumptions, change commercial activity or defer discretionary expenditure.

The objective is not simply another forecast version. It is an understandable comparison of the trade-offs.

>Review and approve

Decision-makers challenge the assumptions, assess uncertainty and agree the response. Authorised users approve the relevant planning changes.

>Explain the outcome

The resulting narrative connects the signal, the financial implications, the options considered and the decision taken.

This scenario illustrates SAP’s broader direction: connecting signals, impact assessment, scenario evaluation and planning actions while maintaining human oversight. It is not a claim that every step is available today as one end-to-end workflow.

6. How the planner’s work changes

The intended transformation is a redistribution of effort, not the removal of planning expertise. Now lets map the traditional planning apporach to embracing Agentic workflows in planning:

Collecting and preparing inputsReviewing input quality, exceptions and business relevance
Building models and calculation logic manuallyDefining requirements and validating generated structures and logic
Searching through reports for issuesInvestigating prioritised deviations and signals
Rebuilding scenariosChallenging assumptions and comparing alternatives
Writing commentary from a blank pageReviewing, refining and contextualising draft explanations
Coordinating disconnected tasksGoverning a more connected decision process

The planner’s role shifts further towards decision support and performance steering, with less time spent assembling the underlying analysis. They will not just be the curator of AI-generated outputs. In my experience, the greatest value comes when finance can spend more time challenging assumptions and shaping the response, not simply explaining the numbers.

It requires financial judgement, operational understanding and the confidence to reject a plausible recommendation when its assumptions do not hold. We NEED to retain that very important human oversight as part of the planning experience.

7. Building on the planning and analytics foundation

Agents should not be presented within the organisation as replacing the capabilities already supporting planning teams.

Models, calculations, forecasting methods, versions, analytics and workflows remain the foundation. SAP Enterprise Planning combines these planning capabilities with natural-language queries, AI-assisted insights and an agentic layer for steering like never before.

A useful distinction is:

  • Analytical and predictive capabilities provide evidence, forecasts and simulations.

  • Assistance helps my planners interact with those capabilities.

  • Agentic workflows coordinate multiple activities around a business objective.

Do you have a strong foundation? This is why the quality of the underlying planning environment matters. Faster execution of an unclear calculation or an inconsistent business definition does not produce a better decision.

8. Trust and governance belong in the design

As assistance extends into planning actions, the questions become more consequential.

Who can create or change a model? Which users can run calculations? Can an agent prepare a proposed update but not publish it? Which actions require approval? How will a reviewer understand the assumptions behind a recommendation?

SAP describes its enterprise planning approach as using governed data products, controlled planning models, access controls and auditable planning outcomes. Those principles still need to be translated into the configuration and operating model of each implementation.

For an initial use case, define:

  • The permitted actions and data access.

  • The assumptions and outputs that require review.

  • The approval boundary before changes become effective.

  • The evidence needed to explain a recommendation.

  • The process for correcting or rejecting an unsuitable result.

Automation and accountability need to develop together.

9. Roadmap and practical preparation

The illustration indicates a phased direction as SAP continues to innovate rapidly in the Enterprise Planning space. It is important for each organisation to be prepared on how to deliver to the business:

A practical preparation sequence could be as follows:

  1. Select a decision-focused use case. For example start with rolling-forecast preparation, scenario evaluation or variance commentary - not just focusing on deploy agents as an objective.

  2. Review the foundation. Check model structures, business definitions, input quality and calculation logic.

  3. Establish approval boundaries. Separate assistance, proposed changes and authorised execution.

  4. Confirm availability and entitlements. Validate release status, prerequisites, licensing and applicable AI consumption requirements.

  5. Measure business value. Track preparation time, scenario turnaround, review effort and decision quality.

As always, roadmap information is forward-looking and subject to change. Use released documentation to confirm functionality and availability.

A Closing perspective

Planning agents offer a way to connect work that has often been fragmented: preparing the model, understanding a deviation, testing a response and explaining a decision.

For FP&A, that creates the potential for more timely financial insight. For Extended and Enterprise-wide planning, it creates the potential to connect that insight with the operational assumptions and actions behind it.

The question is not how much of the planning cycle can be handed to an agent. It is where assistance can improve the quality and speed of a business decision and where human judgement must remain explicit.

Which part of your planning cycle would benefit most from that change, and where would you retain a mandatory human approval?

entry.title: From Innovation to Certification: How SAP Partners Are Turning AI Into Business Outcomes
entry.content:
There is a pattern emerging across the SAP partner ecosystem — and it is worth paying attention to.

Partners who committed early to building AI-powered solutions on SAP Business Technology Platform (SAP BTP), then went the extra mile to validate their work through SAP Certification, are now delivering measurable, real-world impact for their customers. This is not a trend driven by marketing claims. It is a trend driven by results.

Over recent months, a number of remarkable solutions have completed SAP Certification. Each one tells a compelling story of investment, ingenuity, and accountability. Here are five examples — and a time-sensitive opportunity you won't want to miss.

TheValueChain — Transforming Invoice Processing for Allinox

Belgian cookware company Allinox has been perfecting its craft for 120 years. What it did not need to keep perfecting was manual invoice processing. TheValueChain built an AI-powered supplier invoice management solution that reduced processing time from days to minutes, improved accuracy, and freed finance teams to focus on higher-value strategic work — rather than data entry. Learn more

EY — Bringing Generative AI to Contract Management

EY developed EY.ai Contract Authoring, a Generative AI solution built on SAP BTP using machine learning and large language models. The solution automates contract creation, enables intelligent clause extraction, and supports real-time contract formulation across industries. For organizations managing high volumes of complex contracts, this represents a fundamental shift in how legal and commercial work gets done. Learn more

NTT DATA — Making AI Adoption Accessible for Enterprises

One of the biggest barriers to enterprise AI adoption is not ambition — it is complexity. NTT DATA addressed this head-on with GenAI Accelerated, a solution running on SAP BTP that enables rapid configuration and deployment of AI services grounded in real business data. By removing the technical friction between enterprises and AI, NTT DATA is helping organizations move from proof of concept to production at speed. Learn more

KTern.AI — Redefining SAP Migrations with Agentic AI

SAP system migrations have long been resource-intensive, time-consuming, and heavily reliant on institutional knowledge. KTern.AI is changing that. Their agentic AI platform uses multiagent orchestration and reverse engineering within SAP systems to automatically analyze custom developments and generate human-readable documentation for both IT and business teams. Migration projects that once took months of manual analysis can now move significantly faster, with greater transparency at every step. Learn more

TronIT — Solving One of SAP BTP's Most Pressing Infrastructure Challenges

The migration of HTML5 applications from the SAP BTP Neo environment to Cloud Foundry is a challenge many organizations are facing — and dreading. TronIT built the TRON Migration Engine, an AI-guided automation solution that reduces migration effort by hundreds of hours. For SAP customers navigating this transition, it is a lifeline. Learn more

What These Partners Have in Common

None of these partners waited for AI to become mainstream before building. They identified real customer problems, built purposeful solutions on SAP BTP, and then took a critical step that many overlook: they pursued SAP Certification.

SAP Certification is more than a badge. It is a verified signal to customers that a solution meets SAP's quality standards, integrates cleanly into their technology landscape, and is built to last. In a market where "AI-powered" has become a ubiquitous label, certification is what distinguishes credible innovation from noise. It gives customers confidence, and it gives partners a competitive edge that no marketing campaign can replicate.

A Time-Sensitive Opportunity for SAP Partners

If you are an SAP partner with a solution leveraging AI, Clean Core, or SAP BTP — and you have not yet explored certification — now is the moment to act.

SAP Certification for Custom Joule Agents, Intelligent Apps for SAP Business Data Cloud, and Partner Applications on SAP BTP Utilizing Generative AI capabilities is free until the end of the year, with limited slots available.

This is a rare opportunity to earn the full weight of the SAP Certified stamp at no cost. Do not let it pass.

To learn more about SAP Certification and how to get started, reach out to the SAP Integration and Certification Center.

entry.title: Joule Agents on SAP Cloud ERP Private: What Really Happens When You Try to Activate One
entry.content:
There are three ways to get a Joule agent working on SAP Cloud ERP Private. Before any of them matters, there is one check that decides whether a single one of them is open to you.

You have AI Units on the contract. Business Data Cloud is provisioned. Finance has an approved use case and a sponsor.

Someone asks you the obvious question: "We have S/4HANA, Business Data Cloud and AI Units. So which agents do we build in S/4, and which ones on BDC?"

It is a good question from a well prepared team, and it contains a category error. Neither S/4HANA nor Business Data Cloud is a place where agents are built. But that is not the reason the project stalls. You open the agent's Discovery Center page, and the minimum release is SAP S/4HANA 2025 FPS01, restricted to Early Adopter Care. Production is on 2023. Today the answer is not one platform or the other. It is none of the three paths, and nobody in the conversation had mentioned it.

There is also something that has to be settled before any of that, and it is not one of the three paths.

It is the release. On SAP Cloud ERP Private the Autonomous Finance agents require S/4HANA 2025 FPS01, and at the time of writing they are available only to customers enrolled in an Early Adopter Care programme. A landscape below that line has no path to choose yet, whatever else is in place.

Once a landscape is above that line, two things decide which path applies: what the thing has to produce when it finishes, and how far it has to reach to produce it. Answer those and the path picks itself.

So this post does two things. It establishes where to check that first, and then it walks the three paths that the choice is actually between, with one finance process carried along each of them.

Reach drawn as radius. Each path stops at a boundary, and that boundary is the reason the next one exists.

Three words worth getting right

Most of the confusion in these conversations is vocabulary, not architecture.

Term

What it actually is

Joule Assistant

The orchestrator. It takes the user's intent, plans the work, picks which agents to invoke, sequences them, and assembles the answer. It decides the what and the when.

Joule Agent

A task executor with a narrow, pre-defined scope. It decides how to accomplish its objective inside that scope. It does not control the wider flow.

Agent Extension

A Joule Studio solution type. SAP's own description: custom skills, instructions or data fields added to existing SAP agents.

The last one is the one most people have never heard of, and it is the one that resolves the majority of these conversations.

And a second set, because SAP renamed the products

In 2025 SAP renamed its cloud ERP offerings, and the rename is still visible in some places and not others. The old and new names both circulate.

  • SAP Cloud ERP was S/4HANA Cloud, public edition. Multi-tenant, SAP schedules the upgrades, no deferral, standard code cannot be modified. The journey is SAP GROW.
  • SAP Cloud ERP Private was S/4HANA Cloud, private edition. Single tenant, the customer schedules upgrades and can defer them, full ABAP development. The journey is RISE with SAP.
  • SAP HANA Cloud is not ERP at all. It is a managed database service on BTP, and it is what Datasphere and Business Data Cloud sit on. Every S/4HANA system uses a HANA database internally, but that is not the product. A customer who says "we are on HANA Cloud" has told you about their data platform and nothing about their ERP.

That last one matters more than it looks, because the edition decides which agents exist at all.

Path one: activate what SAP already delivers

The test for this path is simple. Does SAP's encoded logic already match how the customer works? If it does, nothing gets built.

Take the SAP Accounting Accruals Agent, reached through the Financial Closing Assistant, as the worked example. Here is what actually happens.

An accountant asks in Joule to prepare accruals for a period and company code. The Assistant routes the intent to the agent. The agent reads two things: the company's own accrual policy handbook, uploaded as a document, and transaction data in the Universal Journal, which includes open purchase orders, goods receipts without an invoice, prepayments and the GR/IR clearing account, plus what is already posted for the period so it does not duplicate. It applies the policy rules against a configured materiality threshold, and produces journal entry proposals, each one carrying a plain-language rationale naming the transactions and the rule it applied.

Those proposals land in the Manage Accrual Proposals Fiori app, where a GL accountant accepts, modifies or rejects each one and posts the accepted entries.

The agent does not post. That is the product, not a configuration choice. That single fact answers most of what a finance team wants to know before it lets an agent near the ledger.

Two things about this flow that surprise people

First, a delivered agent is reading the organisation's own document. Document grounding is not a custom-agent feature. Anyone who assumes that delivered means no local content will reach for a build where an upload would have done.

The handbook has real constraints worth knowing before you promise anything. It is uploaded by asking Joule for it from the Manage Accrual Proposals app. It must be a PDF, it supports a maximum of five expense categories before proposal generation times out, and it must name company codes, expense categories and calculation rules, with everything for a given company code in one document. A new upload overwrites the previous one immediately, with no versioning and no approval workflow, which is worth knowing before a period close depends on it.

Second, the minimum release is per agent, not per product. On SAP Cloud ERP Private the Autonomous Finance agents currently require S/4HANA 2025 FPS01. The SAP Discovery Center pages for the Accounting Accruals Agent and the Receivables and Payables Clearing Agent both state that version, and both list the agent as available only to customers enrolled in an Early Adopter Care programme. SAP Note 3789370 carries the same picture for Private Edition. Check the agent's own page against the system's release rather than relying on a product-level answer.

This path is not a project. It is an activation, a policy document, and training for the people who work the review app. What proves it is one period closed with the agent running alongside the team.

Path two: extend what SAP delivers

The test here is the one that separates most real conversations from imagined ones. Is this the same output, computed by a different rule?

If the customer's process produces the same thing SAP's agent produces but arrives at it differently, you extend. You do not replace.

Agent Extensions are a named solution type in Joule Studio, alongside Agents, n8n Workflows and Applications. SAP's Architecture Center describes what one consists of in a single line: custom skills, instructions or data fields added to existing SAP agents. Three things, named.

Stay with the accruals example and it maps cleanly. Suppose freight accrues off contracted lane rates held in a custom field on the purchase order rather than from the invoice history SAP's logic assumes, and the European company codes sit under a different materiality threshold than the US ones. Neither of those is a new process. Both produce an accrual proposal, reviewed in the same app, posted to the same ledger.

So: a custom data field makes the lane rate visible to the calculation, a custom instruction tiers materiality by company code instead of one global number, and a custom skill calls a control the base agent does not know about.

What the customer keeps

This is the part most often left out of the comparison.

  • SAP's data reads stay as delivered
  • The output is still an accrual proposal, carrying its reasoning
  • The review app and the approval gate are unchanged, so the finance team learns nothing new
  • The base agent stays on SAP's release train

That last point matters more than it looks. Extend, and the agent is positioned to inherit SAP's next version. Rebuild the same thing from scratch and it has to be maintained against every release, which is a cost that shows up in year two rather than year one.

Two honest limits

Extensions do not port between editions. SAP's clean core guidance puts it plainly: extensions created for private edition generally require adaptations to be portable to the public cloud, side-by-side extensions on BTP are more likely to be compatible because they decouple the logic from the core, and complete parity is not guaranteed because API availability and scope differ across editions. There is a second, more practical point at the time of writing. Every published extension tutorial targets a Public Edition agent, and I could not find one that extends a Private Edition agent. Whether that reflects what the catalogue actually offers, or only what has been written up so far, I cannot tell from public sources. Worth checking against your own tenant rather than taking from a post.

And the upgrade behaviour is positioning, not a published guarantee. SAP has built extension as the path that respects the release train, and that is the architectural intent. The mechanism itself is not documented, and extension points appear to be declared per agent rather than universally. Worth confirming for the specific agent rather than assuming it holds generally.

Path three: build in Joule Studio

The test for this one: is the output a different thing entirely?

If what the customer wants does not exist as an SAP business object, no delivered agent will ever produce it, because it is not an SAP process. It is this company's question. That is when you build, and it is the only honest reason to.

Stay with finance and the shape is obvious. The accruals agent produces a proposal. Suppose the CFO wants something else: two weeks before close, what the accrual exposure is likely to land at across the whole group, including commitments sitting in a third-party receivables platform that never enters S/4HANA, compared against the same quarter in prior years that the ERP no longer keeps online.

That is not an accrual proposal. It is a briefing with a recommendation. Different object, so neither activate nor extend can reach it.

What a Joule Studio agent is actually made of

An agent is a definition plus a set of tools, not a programme.

The definition carries a name, a description, its expertise and its instructions, and Joule uses that description to decide when to route a request to it. You select a model available through the generative AI hub. Then you add tools. The assignable tool types today are:

  • Joule Skills, single deterministic actions
  • Actions, API calls to SAP or third-party systems
  • Automations, Build Process Automation workflows
  • Document grounding resource groups
  • MCP server tools, reached over BTP destinations
  • Other custom agents, used as subagents
  • Human-in-the-loop confirmation points, so the agent pauses for approval at the decisions that matter

This is where Business Data Cloud genuinely belongs, and notice that it arrived on the third path rather than the first. A question that spans entities, spans years and spans systems is exactly what the data layer exists for, and almost nothing before this point needed it.

One limit people assume away

A custom agent can use other custom agents as subagents. It cannot call an SAP-delivered agent. The current interoperability model works inbound: a third-party or custom agent can invoke a delivered Joule Agent through the Agent Gateway. The reverse, a Joule Studio agent calling a delivered SAP agent, is a later iteration, and Joule orchestrating mixed chains of delivered and custom agents is planned rather than shipped.

So a design that assumes a new agent will delegate to the Accruals Agent needs checking before it reaches a whiteboard.

One more thing worth stating plainly, because it is the first question anyone responsible for the ledger will ask: a custom agent runs in the calling user's security context. SAP's own product page puts it directly, saying that all agent traffic flows through the agent gateway, so agents can only execute what the end user has permission to do directly. An agent is not a route around access control.

 

One front door, three places the work lands, and only the third reaching outside the ERP.

The boundary nobody checks

Everything above is about choosing a path. This section is about whether the customer's use case is reachable from any of them, and it is the part most often skipped.

An agent activation is scoped to one backend and one client.

The mechanism is the skills mapping. Each agent has pre-defined Joule Skills that map to specific intended back ends, and only back ends with official, delivered skills are eligible targets for that agent's execution. Routing follows the step ownership defined in the delivered process. There is no mechanism for a single active agent to query or route across multiple clients or backend systems within one conversation turn.

Joule can surface agents from different connected systems in the same interface, which is why this is easy to miss. But each agent still executes against the backend its skills were mapped to, and SAP's product page states the permission boundary directly: all agent traffic flows through the agent gateway, so agents can only execute what the end user has permission to do directly.

How many systems one Joule instance can front is a separate question, and SAP's documentation currently disagrees with itself about it. The constraints pages say a Joule instance links to a single S/4HANA system. The Q2 2026 release notes and the Joule Feature Summary Document say Joule supports connecting multiple Private Edition and Public Edition systems within one formation. Until those reconcile it is not a number worth quoting. What holds either way is the agent-level constraint above: whatever Joule can front, an individual agent still executes against one backend.

Why this decides so many conversations

Consider a landscape with one production client live today and further regional clients built and tested but not yet promoted. Everything works. The agent sits in the live client, reads what it needs, proposes, a person posts.

Now the regional waves land. Each client that goes live needs its own activation, and each of those agents executes against its own client. Joule can front all of them, so a user still asks one question and is routed to the right system. What no single agent does is reason across all five in one turn.

One activation per client. Joule fronts all of them; no single agent reasons across them.

So the question that genuinely spans the clients is not answered by any delivered agent, and it is not answered by an extension either, because extending changes the rule and not the reach. It is answerable where those clients converge, which is the data layer. That is the honest case for Business Data Cloud, and it is a better case than the one usually made for it, because it comes from a constraint rather than from a product sheet.

This belongs alongside the release check, before the catalogue is opened at all. A use case whose data sits in another client, another instance, or in a legacy ERP that only replicates financial documents in, is not reachable from the activate path however many AI Units are already paid for.

What this looks like in a real landscape

Abstractions are easy to agree with, so here is the shape of a real estate with its identifying detail removed. Nothing about it is unusual, which is the point.

They run Cloud ERP Private on release 2023, with a second landscape on release 2025 being built in parallel. Production carries one business client. Several further clients exist in quality and development, configured and tested, waiting on the regional rollout. Central Finance is live, replicating financial documents in from legacy ERP systems still running finance in some parts of the world.

Four things follow from that. The first three are checkable; the fourth is a question I could not resolve.

None of the three paths is open to them yet. The finance agents need 2025 FPS01 and Early Adopter Care enrolment, and the business runs on 2023. The second landscape is where the paths become available, so the first move is finishing that migration, not choosing between agents.

The scope ceiling is not hypothetical, it is scheduled. One production client today means one activation and no ceiling felt. When the regional clients are promoted, the ceiling arrives, and it arrives on a date someone has already planned.

Central Finance changes what the agent can see. The accruals agent reads open purchase orders, goods receipts without an invoice, and the GR/IR clearing account. Central Finance replicates financial and controlling postings plus a defined subset of logistics through the accounting view of logistics. That is an accounting view, not the logistics document chain. Whether it satisfies what the agent's logic expects is a real question, and I have not seen it answered publicly. The practical consequence is that processes posted natively in the live client are reachable, and regions still running in a legacy ERP are not.

Almost the whole surrounding stack is already there. Cloud Identity Services, Build Work Zone, the connectivity and destination services, Integration Suite and the Business AI Platform are all live in the production landscape, as are Business Data Cloud and Datasphere. When the release does arrive, this is a configuration exercise rather than a procurement one, which is worth establishing on any landscape early.

Four questions, in order

These work on any process, not only finance, and they take about five minutes.

  1. Which release is it on, and is the agent available there?

The product, the release and the feature pack, then that agent's own Discovery Center page. On Cloud ERP Private the finance agents need 2025 FPS01 and Early Adopter Care enrolment. Below that line there is no path to choose yet, and every question after this one is academic.

  1. What does it produce, and where is the data?

A posted document, a cleared item, a proposal for review, or a briefing. If the output is the same business object SAP's agent already produces, the answer is path one or two. A different object means path three. Then: which client holds the data it needs, because one agent reads one backend and one client.

  1. Is the gap the process, or the rule?

Does SAP's agent do the right job the wrong way, or the wrong job entirely? Right job, wrong way is an extension, and it is usually a few fields and an instruction. Wrong job entirely is the only honest reason to build. This is the question most often skipped, and skipping it is how a few fields and an instruction turn into a project.

  1. Is the outside thing data, or does it decide?

A non-SAP system is either a source you read or a partner that makes its own calls. Reading their data is a connection you configure. Their system deciding on your behalf is a different conversation, and not all of it is available yet.

Most of these conversations open at build, because that is the conversation the market has taught everyone to have. Starting at the release and working down is a shorter route to something that actually ships.

Where the record stops

A post like this is more useful with its edges marked than with them smoothed over. Four things I could not settle.

How an extension survives an upgrade. SAP positions Agent Extensions as the path that respects the release train. The mechanism is not published, and neither is what regression testing a customer still owes at each release. I would treat upgrade safety as architectural intent rather than a guarantee.

Whether Private Edition agents can be extended at all today. Every published extension tutorial I could find targets a Public Edition agent. No public documentation states whether Private Edition agents appear in the extension catalogue, in either direction. This is the gap I would most like someone to close.

Whether Central Finance's accounting view of logistics satisfies an agent that expects the logistics documents themselves. This matters to any customer running Central Finance, which is a large population, and I have not found it addressed.

How many systems one Joule instance fronts. The constraints pages and the Feature Summary Document give different answers, and I could not find which supersedes which. The agent-level scoping is unaffected either way.
